questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis for a Given Null Space
questions.problem: Given that  $\text{Null}(A)={[\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\,:\,{x}_{3}\in R}$, find a basis for $\text{Null}(A).$
questions.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\text{Null}(A)$ has the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Expanding, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, a basis for $\text{Null}(A)$ is

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}
$$

since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate $\text{Null}(A).$

questions.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\text{Null}(A)$ has the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{3}+2{x}_{4} \\ 2{x}_{3}-5{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3},{x}_{4}\in R.
$$

Expanding, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{3}+2{x}_{4} \\ 2{x}_{3}-5{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{4} \\ -5{x}_{4} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore a basis for $\text{Null}(A)$ is

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}
$$

since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate $\text{Null}(A).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis for the Null Space of a Matrix Given in Reduced Row Echelon Form
questions.problem: Find a basis of the null space of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
To find a basis of $\text{Null}(A),$ we need to solve the equation $Ax=0$ and express the solution as a linear combination of linearly independent vectors. Those vectors form a basis of $\text{Null}(A).$

The given matrix is already in reduced row echelon form. So, the equation $Ax=0$ corresponds to the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{4}=0 \\ {x}_{2}+2{x}_{4}=0 \\ {x}_{3}-3{x}_{4}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}={x}_{4} \\ {x}_{2}=-2{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{3}=3{x}_{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, ${x}_{1}$, ${x}_{2}$, and ${x}_{3}$ are basic variables corresponding to the pivot columns ($1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd) and ${x}_{4}$ is a free variable corresponding to the non-pivot column. Therefore, if $x\in \text{Null}(A),$ then

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{4} \\ -2{x}_{4} \\ 3{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}]={x}_{4}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where ${x}_{4}\in R.$ This implies that

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}
$$

is a basis of $\text{Null}(A)$ since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate the $\text{Null}(A).$

$$

$$

To find a basis of $\text{Null}(A),$ we need to solve the equation $Ax=0$ and express the solution as a linear combination of linearly independent vectors. Those vectors form a basis of $\text{Null}(A).$

Since $A∼B,$ the equation $Ax=0$ is equivalent to the equation $Bx=0,$ which corresponds to the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{4}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{4}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{4}$ and ${x}_{2}={x}_{4},$  and ${x}_{3}=0,$ where  ${x}_{4}$ is a free variable. Therefore, if $x\in \text{Null}(A),$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{4} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}]={x}_{4}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,{x}_{4}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}
$$

is a basis of $\text{Null}(A)$ since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate $\text{Null}(A).$

questions.problem: Given the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]$, find a basis of $\text{Null}(A).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $A$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation $Ax=0$ is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}=0,$ where ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. Therefore, if $x\in \text{Null}(A),$ then

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

This implies that 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}
$$

is a basis of $\text{Null}(A)$ since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate $\text{Null}(A).$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}+2{x}_{4}=0 \\ {x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}-{x}_{4}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}-2{x}_{4}$ and ${x}_{2}=-5{x}_{3}+{x}_{4},$ where ${x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}$ are free variables. Therefore, if $x\in \text{Null}(A),$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3}-2{x}_{4} \\ -5{x}_{3}+{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ -5{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{4} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3},{x}_{4}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}
$$

is a basis of $\text{Null}(A)$ since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate $\text{Null}(A).$

First, we reduce the matrix $A$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation $Ax=0$ is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}+2{x}_{4}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is ${x}_{1}=4{x}_{3}-2{x}_{4},$ where ${x}_{2},$ ${x}_{3},$ and ${x}_{4}$ are free variables. Therefore, if $x\in \text{Null}(A),$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3}-2{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{4} \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that 

$$

is a basis of $\text{Null}(A)$ since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate $\text{Null}(A).$

questions.problem: Given the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}]$, find a basis of $\text{Null}(A).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $A$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 9 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, equation $Ax=0$ is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+9{x}_{3}-4{x}_{4}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}+3{x}_{4}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is ${x}_{1}=-9{x}_{3}+4{x}_{4}$ and ${x}_{2}=6{x}_{3}-3{x}_{4},$ where ${x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}$ are free variables. Therefore, if $x\in \text{Null}(A),$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-9{x}_{3}+4{x}_{4} \\ 6{x}_{3}-3{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9{x}_{3} \\ 6{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{4} \\ -3{x}_{4} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 6 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3},{x}_{4}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 6 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}
$$

is a basis of $\text{Null}(A)$ since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate $\text{Null}(A).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Null Space of a Matrix Given a Row Equivalent Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
The matrices $A$ and $B$ are given below. If $A$ is row equivalent to $B$, then find a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064941/assets/5971723fe2da8b35c0c965b25bf084080b2602b52a1099b6c97f637ca62fb2c2.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A),$ we need to solve the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ and express the solution as a linear combination of linearly independent vectors. Those vectors form a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A).$

Since $A\sim B,$ the equation $A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the equation $B\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0},$ which corresponds to the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{4}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is $x_1=0$ and $x_2=\dfrac{1}{3}x_3 - \dfrac{2}{3} x_4$ where $x_3$ and $x_4$ are free variables. Therefore, if $\mathbf{x}\in\textrm{Null}(A),$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3},{x}_{4}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064941/assets/7c7c6711d4453e0e8365dbec263cf23e0c8e4bf05ff091ecc3bf9593797ff538.png)

is a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A)$ since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate $\textrm{Null}(A).$

canonical_examples.problem: Given the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064941/assets/13a1fbdcd6620ab5ccc41283da5ded8996053f9a59fd8c820ea786837ae05222.png) find a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $A$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that the only solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ is $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.$ So $\textrm{Null}(A)=\{ \mathbf{0} \},$ which means that the basis of $\textrm{Null}(A)$ is the empty set, i.e., $\mathcal{B}=\{\,\}.$
